We've already seen multiple examples showing that granting Meta's Muse app full disk access on Mac is a terrible idea, and now another serious privacy issue has come to light. The latest finding is that Muse analyses your communications with every person in your life on an hourly basis.

Apple is right to be concerned about this development, and the company said in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the "full disk access" feature that has been the source of the problem……

Meta's Muse app has made the issue urgent

Meta recently launched its Muse personal AI agent app for iPhone and Mac. Despite the obvious folly of giving a Meta app unrestricted access to everything on your Apple devices, the app still quickly rose to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, things soon went wrong. And they didn't get better afterwards — Wired reported that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered Meta had instructed Muse to extract all the information needed to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be the ability to "create a page for every person in the user's life." This hourly process includes compiling data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people you "follow." The instructions also state: "where they live, what they're doing, recurring topics (moving, shared savings goals)." They add that the model can record "important days" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history could include background information like "March trip, resolved arguments, last week's milestones."

Apple tightens controls on full disk access

You might think the permission prompt for granting an app "full disk access" on Mac is clear enough, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy people have handed over this carte blanche access to their machines without fully understanding how dangerous the step is.

Apple says the feature was originally intended for backup apps, but developers are now using it for many more purposes, including AI agents. The company has said it intends to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when granting this permission.

What Apple must and must not do

Apple considers this step "essential," and I wholeheartedly agree. When existing permission requests don't adequately convey the gravity of what users are agreeing to, Apple has a responsibility to make sure people truly understand what they're allowing.

What I'd like to see is more explicit wording warning people not to proceed unless they're certain of the consequences. Something along the lines of:

Basically, no warning could be too strong. I'd also accept a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

Peter's popular comments

While I find it a bit annoying that Apple periodically asks me whether I want to continue allowing apps to access location data, I do appreciate the approach. At least once, I realised I no longer wanted a particular app to have that level of access. It also reminds me to periodically think about which apps might still be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the mistake it made with screen recording in macOS Sequoia. Of course, that feature is equally extremely dangerous, so the strongest warning is appropriate — but what Apple did was force us to confirm these permissions weekly, and every time after a restart.

This approach was widely condemned as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing a "subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, Apple has already gone too far with the occasional re-confirmation prompts on iPhone. For example, I've already authorised Citymapper to access my location so it can continue providing navigation in the background, so Apple, I really don't need you to ask me again whether I still want to do that.

Yes, issue the strongest possible warning for full disk access, but if someone chooses to proceed, macOS must respect their decision. Please, no more weekly or other forced re-confirmations.
